item.title: A Debtors’ Club for a Fragmented World
item.dc:creator: Ishac Diwan
item.description: The newly created Borrowers’ Platform aims to facilitate knowledge-sharing and capacity-building among debtor countries, while amplifying their voices in global financial circles. But at a time when the Paris Club of sovereign creditors is increasingly unable to act collectively, the Borrowers’ Platform should ramp up its ambition.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto via Getty Images

The newly created Borrowers’ Platform aims to facilitate knowledge-sharing and capacity-building among debtor countries, while amplifying their voices in global financial circles. But at a time when the Paris Club of sovereign creditors is increasingly unable to act collectively, the Borrowers’ Platform should ramp up its ambition.

By Ishac Diwan

BANGKOK—For seven decades, some of the world’s biggest official creditors have coordinated their positions in negotiations with debtor countries struggling with repayment. The Paris Club has sought not only to tackle debt treatment for individual sovereigns, but also to shape the rules governing bailouts and conditionality, largely by leveraging its 22 permanent members’ influence at the International Monetary Fund. Now, the world’s debtors have created a club of their own. The question is whether its stated goals are sufficiently ambitious.

item.title: Trump’s Tariff Fiasco Could Save Free Trade
item.dc:creator: Anne O. Krueger
item.description: US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised prices and hurt businesses without reducing the trade deficit or creating manufacturing jobs. But global trade has held up better than expected, and growing public opposition to tariffs could pave the way for a retreat from protectionism.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised prices and hurt businesses without reducing the trade deficit or creating manufacturing jobs. But global trade has held up better than expected, and growing public opposition to tariffs could pave the way for a retreat from protectionism.

By Anne O. Krueger

WASHINGTON, DC—In the nearly two years since he returned to the White House, US President Donald Trump has picked up where he left off in his first term, shredding the open multilateral trading system that has served the world so well since the end of World War II. He has imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries, repeatedly raising and lowering them and changing rates on individual goods and countries, seemingly on a whim. As a result, US tariff rates are now higher than at any time since the Great Depression’s Smoot-Hawley tariffs.

item.title: If AI Thinks for Us, Democracy Will Suffer
item.dc:creator: John Palfrey
item.description: Whereas the internet buried us in information, AI enables us to outsource analysis altogether. But when it comes to grappling with humanity’s most important questions, we must resist the temptation and recognize that we all have a duty—to each other and to ourselves—to keep “showing up.”
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Patrick Pleul/Picture Alliance via Getty Images

Whereas the internet buried us in information, AI enables us to outsource analysis altogether. But when it comes to grappling with humanity’s most important questions, we must resist the temptation and recognize that we all have a duty—to each other and to ourselves—to keep “showing up.”

By John Palfrey

CHICAGO—Sometime in the 18th century, the Enlightenment settled a contentious, centuries-old question: Where does knowledge come from? For millennia, many people had pointed to God. But the early modern period brought a new consensus, namely that knowledge comes from human scientists working at the edge of what is known, armed with observation, mathematics, experimentation, and logic.

item.title: A Tory Mentor for the MAGA GOP
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Strain
item.description: Kemi Badenoch’s keynote address at the British Conservative Party conference last month outlined her plan for a pro-growth future that respects fiscal discipline and human dignity. As American conservatives look beyond Donald Trump and to the 2028 primary campaign, they should embrace a similar agenda.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Nicola Tree/Getty Images

Kemi Badenoch’s keynote address at the British Conservative Party conference last month outlined her plan for a pro-growth future that respects fiscal discipline and human dignity. As American conservatives look beyond Donald Trump and to the 2028 primary campaign, they should embrace a similar agenda.

By Michael R. Strain

WASHINGTON, DC—“There is a fight coming in British politics. A fight that we have not seen in this country for more than half a century. It will be a battle for the soul of this nation. A battle of ideas. A battle that goes to the very core of who we are and what kind of country we want to be.”

item.title: The Politics of Poland’s Judicial Crisis
item.dc:creator: Maciej Kisilowski
item.description: The removal of Bogdan Święczkowski as president of the Constitutional Tribunal has triggered a physical confrontation at the court and a political standoff between Donald Tusk’s government and the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party. But Święczkowski was not so much removed as barred, because he held the position illegally.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Omar Marques/Getty Images

The removal of Bogdan Święczkowski as president of the Constitutional Tribunal has triggered a physical confrontation at the court and a political standoff between Donald Tusk’s government and the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party. But Święczkowski was not so much removed as barred, because he held the position illegally.

By Maciej Kisilowski

WARSAW—Dramatic scenes are playing out at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal amid a wave of speculation about whether Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government and the Tribunal judges elected by its liberal parliamentary majority are acting lawfully. Many will ask whether democrats must break the law to restore institutions sabotaged by populist authoritarians. In the Polish case, it’s the wrong question.

item.title: Mapping AI Resistance
item.dc:creator: Carl Benedikt Frey
item.description: Since a society that is reluctant to deploy a technology will not capture its gains, it is worth understanding why the AI revolution is being welcomed in some places and resisted in others. The explanation is not as simple as headline poll data and much media coverage suggest.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: API/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images

Since a society that is reluctant to deploy a technology will not capture its gains, it is worth understanding why the AI revolution is being welcomed in some places and resisted in others. The explanation is not as simple as headline poll data and much media coverage suggest.

By Carl Benedikt Frey

OXFORD—The United States is both the home of the AI revolution and among the places where people like the technology the least. According to Ipsos’s 2026 AI Monitor, 85% of respondents in China, 80% in India, and 77% in Indonesia think that AI products and services offer more benefits than drawbacks, compared to only 38% in the US, with similarly low shares in Britain, France, and the Netherlands.

item.title: The World’s Perilous Ebola Complacency
item.dc:creator: Tom Achoki, Nebiyu Dereje and Jean Kaseya
item.description: The exponential trajectory of the latest Ebola outbreak is an urgent reminder that infectious diseases do not wait for ideal geopolitical alignments or balanced budgets. Global leaders must fund the Africa-led regional response today, or risk paying an immeasurably higher price in human lives and economic devastation tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Jospin Mwisha/AFP via Getty Images

The exponential trajectory of the latest Ebola outbreak is an urgent reminder that infectious diseases do not wait for ideal geopolitical alignments or balanced budgets. Global leaders must fund the Africa-led regional response today, or risk paying an immeasurably higher price in human lives and economic devastation tomorrow.

By Tom Achoki, Nebiyu Dereje and Jean Kaseya

NAIROBI—A catastrophic threat is exploding in the heart of Africa. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is currently battling the deadliest, fastest-moving Ebola outbreak in its history. In mid-May, the World Health Organization and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention declared a public health emergency of international concern and continental security. As of October 27, there were 10,193 cases and 4,960 deaths.

item.title: Industrial Decarbonization Is Good for Business
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth Reynolds and Nathan Collett
item.description: With major governments showing open hostility toward climate solutions or focusing on other needs, one might think that progress toward decarbonization is in jeopardy. Yet across the global industrial sector, many companies are increasing productivity, boosting revenue growth, and reducing emissions all at once.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Scott Olson/Getty Images

With major governments showing open hostility toward climate solutions or focusing on other needs, one might think that progress toward decarbonization is in jeopardy. Yet across the global industrial sector, many companies are increasing productivity, boosting revenue growth, and reducing emissions all at once.

By Elisabeth Reynolds and Nathan Collett

BOSTON—It is not easy to be optimistic about climate change nowadays. In the United States, President Donald Trump’s administration has eliminated incentives for clean-energy investment, slashed funding for numerous private-sector projects, and rescinded long-standing rules limiting greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions from vehicles and power plants. Even in Europe, a longtime climate-policy leader, deadlines are being pushed back and compliance obligations reduced as other challenges, like the war in Ukraine, take priority.

Fortunately, these developments do not tell the whole story. The global industrial sector, which generates about one-third of GHG emissions, is quietly making significant progress. Over the past year, our team at MIT has looked closely at multinational companies that are pursuing industrial decarbonization strategies despite global headwinds. What we frequently found were firms that are increasing productivity, boosting revenue growth, and reducing emissions all at once.

For example, in Fort Worth, Texas, Siemens has harnessed the boom in demand for data-center components to scale up operations, leading to productivity improvements and lower unit costs. And that, in turn, has made increased decarbonization expenditures acceptable to senior leadership and plant directors. Despite the serious environmental concerns about data centers, they do appear to come with a silver lining. Though hyperscalers would prefer not to pay a “green premium,” they also recognize the value of lower-emissions manufacturing processes that reduce energy demand and costs.

Similarly, near Montreal, Saint-Gobain’s construction materials facility received public subsidies for investments in electrification and digital-technology upgrades that led to a plant with zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions (meaning direct emissions and indirect ones tied to a firm’s suppliers). In this case, incentives to promote clean energy led not only to a reduction in emissions but also to competitively priced, higher-quality green products for customers who, all things being equal, will choose the cleaner option.

Two more examples are Outokumpu of Finland, which has a steel facility in Alabama, and the National Cement Company, a subsidiary of the French company Vicat. A combination of factors, including lower environmental and labor standards, makes it difficult for these firms to compete directly with dominant global producers. But under the rules of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and regulations in California designed to support local cement production, both are innovating and developing clean production technologies to maintain long-term competitiveness. Their respective strategies recognize that climate change is a generational issue that governments and companies will have to address sooner or later.

These case studies all show how industrial enterprises are clearing a higher bar than “green for green’s sake.” Such strategies are exactly what we need, because green initiatives can no longer be pursued independently of concerns about growth, security, and competitiveness.

Our research shows that firms often assess their investments at the project level. Individual facilities measure progress holistically, assessing how the cost of inputs (materials, labor, and machinery) stacks up against their target return on investment. It is this approach that allows them to invest in higher-cost technologies when economies of scale, supportive public policies, or both make it possible to pursue decarbonization.

Broader trends support these findings. Global investment in clean energy has increased by approximately 80% in the past decade, outpacing investment in fossil fuels by nearly two to one in the past year. In the US, recent estimates suggest that three-quarters of the clean-energy capacity that was in the works before Trump’s return to the White House will still get built. Two-thirds of the expected emissions reduction from electricity generation will still be achieved.

A green-product premium does help where it exists. But even without one, companies see benefits to pursuing clean energy. Concerns about energy security and costs, and the public backlash over data-center energy use, all provide tailwinds for companies moving toward a greener footprint. Companies also report that a commitment to lower emissions helps attract and retain talent.

Of course, many industries remain resistant—oil and gas most obviously—and the up-front costs of the transition are real. But so, too, is the momentum behind industrial decarbonization. As temperatures keep rising, catastrophic weather events will grow more frequent and severe. Forward-looking companies understand that innovation in advanced manufacturing and clean energy, aided by AI and robotics, creates opportunities for more productive, resilient, and sustainable operations. They also know that interest in clean energy among their customers, communities, and employees is only increasing.

If all this is happening despite the federal government’s open hostility to decarbonization within the world’s most dynamic economy, just think about what we could see under a well-crafted clean-energy strategy. No one knows what the next turn in US politics will bring, but sooner or later, there will be an opportunity for a renewed federal commitment to industrial decarbonization. Then we can build on all the strategies that are already bearing fruit, aligning public- and private-sector interests around the shared goals of growth, competitiveness, and security.

The transition to clean energy may have started as a virtuous exercise. But it is succeeding because it is a winning business strategy.

Elisabeth Reynolds, former Special Assistant to the President for Manufacturing and Economic Development at the National Economic Council (2021–22), is Professor of Practice at MIT’s Department of Urban Studies and Planning.

Nathan Collett is a former Canadian public servant on issues of economic security and a graduate of MIT’s Technology and Policy Program.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: When the AI Bubble Bursts
item.dc:creator: William H. Janeway
item.description: Speculative bubbles often leave behind valuable infrastructure while bankrupting the investors who financed them. AI could follow the same path, but the industry’s growing reliance on borrowed money raises the risk of a major financial crisis long before its world-beating applications emerge.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Speculative bubbles often leave behind valuable infrastructure while bankrupting the investors who financed them. AI could follow the same path, but the industry’s growing reliance on borrowed money raises the risk of a major financial crisis long before its world-beating applications emerge.

By William H. Janeway

CAMBRIDGE—About a year ago, the idea that speculative investment has created an “AI bubble” began to take hold and soon became conventional wisdom. Since bubbles always burst, the fear now is that time is running out for this one.

But no single election can guarantee democracy’s resilience, and the challenges these countries’ new governments face remain formidable.

The recent electoral defeat of far-right forces in Brazil and Serbia offers important lessons for pro-democracy forces around the world as they confront nationalist and illiberal movements. item.title: The Big Picture
item.dc:creator: PS editors
item.content:encoded:
By PS editors

While far-right parties have lately gained ground in some countries, such as Germany, voters have repudiated right-wing leaders in a few notable elections this year. In April, Hungary’s center-right Tisza party won a decisive victory over Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s ruling Fidesz party. And this month, Serbia’s student-led opposition ousted Aleksandar Vučić from power after 14 years of authoritarian rule, and incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva unexpectedly defeated his far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

item.title: The New Geopolitics of Mining
item.dc:creator: Ngaire Woods
item.description: While the US and China want their critical-mineral investments to deliver the biggest returns possible, governments in resource-rich countries must balance external pressures with internal demands. Mining firms must also win local communities’ trust, as host countries will be quick to throw them under the bus if public opinion sours.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Mauro Pimentel/AFP via Getty Images

While the US and China want their critical-mineral investments to deliver the biggest returns possible, governments in resource-rich countries must balance external pressures with internal demands. Mining firms must also win local communities’ trust, as host countries will be quick to throw them under the bus if public opinion sours.

By Ngaire Woods

OXFORD—Two tumultuous elections have captured headlines this week. In Brazil, incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. And in Serbia, the student-led opposition ousted Aleksandar Vučić after 14 years in power. But the challenge for these new governments is just beginning. Whether they like it or not, both will be swept up in the global scramble for critical minerals and metals.

item.title: Can Bond Vigilantes Prevent the Next Debt Crisis?
item.dc:creator: Nouriel Roubini
item.description: With interest rates on government debt having gone from near zero to much higher levels in recent years, rising short- and long-term bond yields have cast doubt on the sustainability of some debts and led many to wonder if a crisis might be looming. While some countries are more protected than others, none is immune.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Spencer Platt/Getty Images

With interest rates on government debt having gone from near zero to much higher levels in recent years, rising short- and long-term bond yields have cast doubt on the sustainability of some debts and led many to wonder if a crisis might be looming. While some countries are more protected than others, none is immune.

By Nouriel Roubini

NEW YORK—Large, growing budget deficits and rising public debt-to-GDP ratios in advanced economies are rattling markets. With interest rates on government debt having gone from near zero (and even negative, in some cases) to much higher levels, rising short- and long-term bond yields have cast doubt on the sustainability of some public debts and led many to ask if a crisis might be looming.

item.title: A Wealth Tax Would Harm California
item.dc:creator: Laura Tyson and Lenny Mendonca
item.description: Before approving a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in the state at a certain point in time, Californians should consider what such a policy will do to future tax revenues. Since wealth is mobile, those who stand to lose the most will simply leave, taking their future income-tax payments with them.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

Before approving a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in the state at a certain point in time, Californians should consider what such a policy will do to future tax revenues. Since wealth is mobile, those who stand to lose the most will simply leave, taking their future income-tax payments with them.

By Laura Tyson and Lenny Mendonca

BERKELEY—Six Nobel laureate economists recently signed an open letter supporting Proposition 40, California’s Billionaire Tax Act, which, if passed by a simple majority of voters, would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of an estimated 250 individuals with a net worth exceeding $1 billion who resided in California on January 1, 2026. We believe the proposal is poorly designed and likely to do more harm than good.

item.title: A Future for Europe’s Youth
item.dc:creator: Ana Palacio
item.description: The current generation of young Europeans possesses freedoms, material resources, opportunities to travel, and technological capabilities beyond anything previous generations could have imagined. Their demands, however, are strikingly simple: decent schools, secure jobs, affordable homes, and the possibility of raising a family.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images

The current generation of young Europeans possesses freedoms, material resources, opportunities to travel, and technological capabilities beyond anything previous generations could have imagined. Their demands, however, are strikingly simple: decent schools, secure jobs, affordable homes, and the possibility of raising a family.

By Ana Palacio

MADRID—At first glance, the wave of student-led protests that has swept across France might resemble the events of May 1968. Both featured surging crowds of demonstrators calling for education reform, criticizing the government, erecting blockades, and being confronted by riot police. Both also attracted casseurs, who turn protest into destruction. But whereas the students of 1968 were seeking to overturn the established order, today’s protesters want the established order to deliver for them.

item.title: A Tale of Two Chinas
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Rogoff
item.description: China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: CN-STR/AFP via Getty Images

China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.

By Kenneth Rogoff

CAMBRIDGE—Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the United States, with Europe trailing far behind. On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

item.title: Sino–American Stability?
item.dc:creator: Stephen S. Roach
item.description: Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images

Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.

By Stephen S. Roach

SHANGHAI—My search for truth inside China has been stymied. Banned from the China Development Forum (CDF), after participating for 25 years as the longest-attending foreign delegate, I feel like an outsider in what was once the country’s most prestigious international gathering. Deteriorating relations with former friends in Hong Kong, some of whom avoid eye contact with me now, have not helped matters. In both cases, I was cut off after offering constructive criticism—highlighting structural malaise in the mainland economy and a loss of autonomous identity in Hong Kong—the essence of what we call debate in the West.

item.title: Europe’s Winter of Discontent
item.dc:creator: Harold James
item.description: Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.

By Harold James

PRINCETON—The postwar architects of European integration notoriously relied on crisis conditions to build more extensive institutions. By contrast, for incremental, piecemeal reforms to succeed, the challenges Europe faces must be relatively small. That hardly describes Europe’s current predicament.

item.title: How Students Dethroned Serbia’s Strongman
item.dc:creator: Filip Milačić
item.description: Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Andrej Isakovic/AFP via Getty Images

Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.

By Filip Milačić

VIENNA—After 14 years of authoritarian rule, Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have been ousted from power. Although polls had predicted a close election, the student-led opposition ultimately won by a wide margin. In an election that was neither free nor fair—owing to media capture, violence against the government’s opponents, and the SNS’s blatant misuse of state resources—the Student List won 53% of the popular vote, which translated into 141 parliamentary seats and an absolute majority. Vučić and his SNS trailed badly, with 38.8% and 103 seats.

item.title: What a US-China AI Safety Channel Needs
item.dc:creator: Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin
item.description: Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Li Zhipeng/Xinhua via Getty Images

Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.

By Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin

WASHINGTON, DC—The most concrete outcome from last month’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was an apparent agreement to set up a US-China AI incident-reporting channel. But even if either government proves willing to use this direct line or start sending data across the Pacific, they must first address a more pressing issue: US and Chinese frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they would need.
